cli/access-billing:
## API keys

```bash
miosa api-key create my-key --preset cli
miosa api-key list
miosa api-key presets
miosa api-key rotate <key>
miosa api-key update <key> --name renamed --rate-limit 600
miosa api-key rm <key> --yes
```

`api-key create` takes `--preset` (`read-only`, `ci`, `agent` or `cli`), `--scope` (repeatable, for example `sandboxes:exec`), `--expires-in` (days), `--rate-limit`, `--allowed-ip` (repeatable), `--workspace-id` and `--quiet-key` (print only the secret).

Scoped keys for external users:

```bash
miosa api-key scoped --external-user-id <id> --workspace-id <id> --scope sandboxes:exec --expires-at 2027-01-01T00:00:00Z
```

## Service accounts

Non-human accounts that own API keys for pipelines and programs.

```bash
miosa service-account new deploy-pipeline
miosa service-account list
miosa service-account key new <account> --preset ci --expires-in 90 --quiet-key
miosa service-account keys <account>
miosa service-account update <account> --description "..." --name renamed
miosa service-account rm <account> --yes
```

`service-account key new` takes the same scoping flags as `api-key create`.

## Webhooks

Send events to your own HTTPS endpoints.

```bash
miosa webhook create https://example.com/hook --name deploys --event sandbox.created
miosa webhook list
miosa webhook get <webhook>
miosa webhook events
miosa webhook deliveries <webhook>
miosa webhook test <webhook>
miosa webhook replay <webhook> <delivery>
miosa webhook update <webhook> --active --event sandbox.created --retries 5
miosa webhook rm <webhook> --yes
```

`webhook create` takes `--event` (repeatable, see `webhook events`), `--header NAME=VALUE` (repeatable), `--retries` (0 to 10) and `--workspace-id`.

## Members

```bash
miosa member list
miosa member add <email> --role member
miosa member role <member> --role admin
miosa member rm <member> --yes
```

Roles are `admin`, `member` or `viewer`.

## Billing

```bash
miosa billing plan
miosa billing balance
miosa billing spend
miosa billing usage
miosa billing breakdown
miosa billing invoices
miosa billing upcoming
miosa billing transactions -n 50 --page 1
```

`miosa billing usage` shows model usage by day and takes no filters. To filter the product catalog by `--product`, `--size`, `--state` or `--template`, use `miosa catalog`.

## Audit log

```bash
miosa audit -n 50 --type sandbox.created --workspace-id <id>
```

## Alerts and notifications

```bash
miosa alerts list
miosa alerts resolve <alert>

miosa notifications list
miosa notifications unread
miosa notifications read <notification>
miosa notifications read-all
```

> **Note**
>
> Billing reads the organization new machines bill. Pin it with `miosa org bill <org>`, or override per command with `--org`. See [Account and environment](/docs/cli/account).
cli/account:
## Who you are

```bash
miosa whoami
```

Shows the user, organization, workspace, plan, credits and the scopes the key holds.

## Organization

The organization is who pays for new machines. `miosa org` shows it and manages its members.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `miosa org` | The organization new machines bill, with members and limits |
| `miosa org list` | Organizations you can bill |
| `miosa org bill [org]` | Pin the organization new machines bill |
| `miosa org bill --clear` | Stop pinning an organization |
| `miosa org members` | Members of the organization |
| `miosa org invite <email> --role member` | Invite a person (`owner`, `admin` or `member`) |
| `miosa org caps` | Show member caps |

`--org` on any command overrides the pinned organization for that command:

```bash
miosa --org acme list
miosa --org acme create build-box
```

Member caps limit what one person can spend or run:

```bash
miosa org caps set dana --spend 25            # dollars per billing period
miosa org caps set dana --concurrent 10       # most machines at once
miosa org caps set dana --no-spend-cap
miosa org caps set dana --no-concurrency-cap
```

## Limits

```bash
miosa limits
```

Shows the limits of the organization a new machine would bill.

## Open the console

```bash
miosa open            # open the web console in a browser
miosa open --print    # print the URL instead
```

## Version and updates

```bash
miosa version
miosa update          # download and replace the binary
miosa update --check  # report only
```

## Doctor

```bash
miosa doctor
```

Checks configuration, connectivity and authentication, and prints a fix for each failure.

> **Note**
>
> Members and their roles live under `miosa member` for day to day changes, and under the organization for invites and caps. API keys and service accounts live under their own pages: [Access, org and billing](/docs/cli/access-billing).
cli/agents:
## Bring your own model

Agent runs use your own model-provider connections, never MIOSA platform keys. Mint a key that can do this with `miosa api-key create NAME --preset cli`. Add a connection with `miosa connections add models` (the key is read from a prompt or stdin, never from an argument). A run without a usable connection fails with a message that names this command.

```bash
miosa api-key create agent-key --preset cli
miosa connections add models
```

## Prompt

Run an agent on a sandbox or computer and follow it.

```bash
miosa prompt --sandbox my-box "fix the failing test"
miosa prompt --new-machine --harness codex "write a README"
miosa prompt --sandbox my-box --continue
```

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-s, --sandbox string` | Sandbox to run in (default: the current sandbox) |
| `--computer string` | Computer to run in |
| `--agent string` | Run a saved agent (name or id) instead of an ad hoc one |
| `--harness string` | `claude-code`, `codex` or `osa` (default: the agent's, or `claude-code`) |
| `--model string` | Model for the harness (default: the harness default) |
| `--new-machine` | Provision a machine for this run |
| `--machine string` | Kind of new machine: `sandbox` or `computer` |
| `--size string` | Size of a new machine |
| `--template string` | Template of a new machine |
| `--chat string` | Chat id; continues the chat if it has runs |
| `--new-chat` | Start a chat (a new chat id is printed) |
| `--reuse string` | New machine lifetime: `run` (one per run) or `chat` (one per `--chat`, files persist) |
| `--after-run string` | What happens to a new machine when the run ends: `destroy`, `pause` or `keep` |
| `--max-time int` | Stop the run after this many seconds |
| `--no-follow` | Print the run id and return without waiting |
| `--notify-email` | Email you when the run finishes |
| `--notify-webhook string` | Webhook id to notify when the run finishes |

## Saved agents

An agent is a saved, versioned definition: harness, model, instructions, the machine it runs on, and what it may do. `<agent>` is a name or an id.

```bash
miosa agent new reviewer --harness claude-code --instructions-file review.md
miosa agent publish reviewer --file config.yaml
miosa agent list
miosa agent diff reviewer 2 3
miosa agent run reviewer "review PR 42" --sandbox my-box
miosa agent harnesses
```

`miosa agent new` takes `--harness` (`claude-code`, `codex`, `osa` or `custom`), `--model`, `--instructions` or `--instructions-file`, `--overdrive` (run the harness without approval prompts), `--timeout-sec`, `--description`, and a full `--file` (YAML or JSON).

Other subcommands: `agent get`, `agent versions`, `agent version`, `agent update`, `agent duplicate`, `agent rm`, `agent runs`, `agent templates`, `agent triggers`, `agent approvals`, `agent authority`, `agent defaults`, `agent harness-versions`.

## Runs

List, follow and stop agent runs.

```bash
miosa run list --status running
miosa run get <id>
miosa run follow <id>
miosa run events <id>
miosa run logs <id>
miosa run messages <id>
miosa run outputs <id>
miosa run files <id>
miosa run diagnostics <id>
miosa run download <id> -O out.tar
miosa run steer --sandbox my-box "also add tests"   # queue the next turn for the running agent
miosa run interrupt --sandbox my-box                # stop the agent attached to a machine
miosa run stop <id>
miosa run usage --group-by model
```

`miosa run list` filters with `--agent-id`, `--chat`, `--harness`, `--source`, `--status`, `--target`, `--workspace-id` and `--limit`.

## Chats

Chats are agent conversations that remember.

```bash
miosa chat list
miosa chat start --sandbox my-box --harness claude-code
miosa chat show <chat-id>
miosa chat context <chat-id>     # how full the context is
miosa chat compact <chat-id>     # compact it so the chat can go on
```

## Connections

Model providers, apps and tool servers your agents use.

```bash
miosa connections add models
miosa connections list --kind models
miosa connections test <name>
miosa connections share <name>
miosa connections rm <name>
```

`miosa connections add` takes `--key-stdin` (never a key on the command line), `--label`, `--workspace-id`, `--url` (for an MCP tool server) and `--header-env HEADER=ENV_VAR` (repeatable).

> **Note**
>
> Runs are the canonical agent execution contract. `miosa prompt`, `miosa agent run` and `miosa chat` all create runs; `miosa run` reads and controls them.
cli/api:
`miosa api` sends a request to the MIOSA API with your stored credentials and prints the response body. The path is relative to the API base URL (`/api/v1`). Use it for anything the CLI has no command for yet.

```bash
miosa api [METHOD] <path> [flags]
```

The method defaults to GET, or POST when `--data` is given.

```bash
miosa api /credits/balance
miosa api GET /sandboxes/my-box/ports
miosa api POST /webhooks -d '{"url":"https://example.com/hook","events":["sandbox.ready"]}'
miosa api PATCH /sandboxes/my-box/tags -d @tags.json
echo '{"name":"x"}' | miosa api POST /workspaces -d -
```

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-X, --method string` | HTTP method (default GET, or POST with `--data`) |
| `-d, --data string` | Request body: JSON, `@file`, or `-` for stdin |
| `-H, --header stringArray` | Extra header, `'Name: value'` (repeatable) |
| `-i, --include` | Print the status line and response headers first |

A failing status exits non-zero (see exit codes) and still prints the body.

## When to reach for the raw API

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Code/build/test/runtime workspace | `miosa create`, `miosa exec`, `miosa files`, `miosa services`, `miosa url` |
| Full GUI/browser computer | `miosa api /computers ...` or an SDK (`client.computers`) |
| Docker Host appliance | SDK or API Docker Host endpoints; publish from a sandbox to Docker Host |
| Product/template readiness | `miosa catalog` |
| Anything else | `miosa api <METHOD> <path>` |

> **Tip**
>
> `miosa api` uses the same profile, key and organization as every other command. Combine it with `--json` and `jq` for scripting. See [JSON output and scripting](/docs/cli/scripting).
cli/cli-vs-mcp:
CLI & MCP

Two ways into the same platform, with the same API key and the same scopes. Pick the one your client can run.

[CLI overview](/docs/cli)[MCP overview](/docs/mcp)[Install the CLI](/docs/cli/install)[MCP tools](/docs/mcp/tools)

- The **CLI** (`miosa`) is for humans, scripts and agents with a shell. You type commands, read text or JSON, and branch on exit codes.
- **MCP** gives AI clients (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Claude Desktop) the same capabilities as tools. The model calls tools by name instead of running shell commands.

Both use the **same API key and the same scopes**. A key that can create a sandbox from the CLI can create one over MCP, and the reverse. The only difference is the surface.

## Which should an agent use?

- **Has a shell? Use the CLI.** Claude Code, Codex, Cursor's terminal and any CI job can run `miosa`. The CLI is often the better choice: it reaches the whole platform, not just one tool surface; output is scriptable; and it composes with `jq`, pipes and files.
- **No shell? Use MCP.** Claude Desktop chat and other hosted chat products have no shell, so tools are the only path. MCP lets the model call capabilities by name.

Nothing is lost either way, because the key, the scopes and the resources are identical.

## Comparison

| | CLI | MCP |
|---|---|---|
| Who drives it | A person, a script, or an agent with a shell | An AI client without a shell (Claude Desktop), or one that prefers tools |
| Interface | `miosa <command> [flags]` | JSON-RPC tools over Streamable HTTP or stdio |
| Install | npm, Homebrew, install script, Releases | Hosted endpoint, no install, or `pip install miosa-mcp` |
| Output | Text or JSON, with exit codes | Structured tool results and images |
| Coverage | The whole platform, plus `miosa api` for any endpoint | The MCP tool surface |
| Best for | Agents with shell access, build loops, CI, one-off operations | Clients without a shell |
| Auth | `msk_u_*` key or a profile | `msk_u_*` key as a Bearer token |
| Scope model | Same key scopes | Same key scopes |

## Use both

A common split: an agent with a shell drives the platform with the CLI, and a client without a shell reaches the same account over MCP with the same key.

```bash
ID=$(miosa create agent-box --size small --wait --json | jq -r .id)   # CLI, from a shell agent
miosa exec "$ID" -- npm test
# the same account over MCP: exec(sandbox_id=ID, command="npm run build")
miosa list --json | jq -r '.data[].name'                              # CLI, read back
```

- [CLI overview](/docs/cli): Install, command groups, global flags and exit codes.
- [MCP overview](/docs/mcp): Connect Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Claude Desktop.

> **Note**
>
> Both surfaces inherit the same tenant scoping, plan limits, credit checks and audit logging, because both sit in front of the MIOSA REST API.
cli/config:
Settings live in `~/.miosa/config.toml` (mode 0600). The API key is never printed by `config`; sign in with `miosa login`.

## Config commands

```bash
miosa config list            # effective settings of the current profile (alias ls)
miosa config get <key>       # print one setting
miosa config set <key> <value>
miosa config path            # print the config file path
```

Keys: `api_url`, `current_sandbox`, `default_workspace`.

```toml
api_url           = "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1"
api_key           = "msk_u_..."
default_workspace = "default"
current_sandbox   = "my-box"
```

## Profiles

A profile is a named sign-in with its own API URL, organization and defaults. Several profiles let you keep accounts or environments apart.

```bash
miosa login --profile work
miosa profile list
miosa profile use work
miosa --profile default list
```

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `miosa profile add <name>` | Create an empty profile (then `miosa login --profile <name>`) |
| `miosa profile list` | List profiles (alias `ls`) |
| `miosa profile show [name]` | Show a profile's settings (the key is masked) |
| `miosa profile use <name>` | Make a profile the default for new commands |
| `miosa profile rm <name>` | Delete a profile and its stored key |

`miosa profile add` takes `--api-url` and `--workspace`.

### Which profile is in effect

1. `--profile`
2. `MIOSA_PROFILE`
3. the one set with `miosa profile use`
4. `default`

## Credential resolution

1. `--api-key`
2. `MIOSA_API_KEY`
3. the active profile in `~/.miosa/config.toml`

## Environment variables

```text
MIOSA_API_KEY          API key
MIOSA_BASE_URL         API base URL
MIOSA_PROFILE          Profile to use
MIOSA_ORG              Organization to bill
MIOSA_OUTPUT           Output format (text or json)
MIOSA_RETRIES          Retries on 429 and transient 5xx
MIOSA_NO_UPDATE_NOTICE Set to 1 to silence the new-version notice
```

## Sign out

```bash
miosa logout                # remove the stored key of the active profile
miosa logout --all          # delete the config file (all profiles)
```

> **Note**
>
> `miosa doctor` checks configuration, connectivity and authentication, and prints a fix for each failure.
cli/devices:
A device is any runtime MIOSA can run a command on: a sandbox, a computer or another kind. `miosa device` is one surface over all of them, so a script does not need to know which kind it is talking to. `<device>` is an id.

```bash
miosa device list
miosa device list --status running
miosa device capabilities <device>
miosa device exec <device> -- uname -a
```

Aliases: `devices`.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `miosa device list` | List devices (`-n, --limit`, `--name`, `--status`) |
| `miosa device get <device>` | Show one device (alias `show`) |
| `miosa device capabilities <device>` | What this device can do (alias `caps`) |
| `miosa device exec <device>` | Run a command (`-c, --command`, `--timeout-ms`) |
| `miosa device files <device>` | List a directory (`--path`, default `/workspace`; alias `ls`) |
| `miosa device read <device>` | Read a file, base64 (`--path`) |
| `miosa device write <device>` | Write a file (`--path`, `--content`, or `--file`) |
| `miosa device expose <device> <port>` | Publish a port |
| `miosa device browser <device>` | Show a device's browser URL (computers) |
| `miosa device extend <device>` | Replace the time to live (`--timeout`, for example `30m` or `2h`) |
| `miosa device pause <device>` / `resume <device>` | Pause or resume |
| `miosa device stop <device>` | Stop, keeping the disk |
| `miosa device rm <device> --yes` | Destroy permanently (aliases `delete`, `destroy`) |

## exec

```bash
miosa device exec <device> -- uname -a
miosa device exec <device> -c "npm test" --timeout-ms 120000
```

`miosa device exec` exits with the remote command's status, like `miosa exec`.

## Files

```bash
miosa device files <device> --path /workspace
miosa device read <device> --path /workspace/out.json
miosa device write <device> --path /workspace/app.py --content "print(1)"
```

`miosa device read` returns the file contents base64-encoded. `miosa device write` takes the contents from `--content`, or a JSON body with `--file`.

## When to use device or the typed command

Use `miosa device` when a script should work across runtime kinds, or when you have an id and do not know what it is. Use `miosa exec`, `miosa files` or `miosa computer` when you know the kind and want the fuller, kind-specific surface.

> **Note**
>
> Machines are also addressable by name in the typed commands (`miosa exec my-box -- ...`). `miosa device` takes an id. See [Machines and lifecycle](/docs/cli/machines).
cli/environments:
An environment is the template a new sandbox or computer starts from. It decides which repositories are cloned, which variables and secret files are injected, and which of your credentials the machine may use. Every workspace has one default environment named `base`. A machine without `--env` uses the default of its workspace.

## Commands

```bash
miosa env list
miosa env new staging
miosa env info staging
miosa env rename staging stage
miosa env rm staging
miosa env default
```

Commands that edit one environment take `--env <name>`, and edit the default environment when it is omitted. `--workspace <slug>` scopes any `miosa env` command to one workspace. Without it the API uses the workspace of a workspace-bound key, and the organization level otherwise.

## Variables and secret files

```bash
miosa env set --env staging STRIPE_KEY       # value is asked for, input hidden
miosa env set --env staging --from-file .env
miosa env unset --env staging STRIPE_KEY
miosa env file put --env staging hello-world/backend/.env ./backend.env
miosa env info staging                        # masked
miosa env info staging --reveal               # print values; written to the audit log
```

A value is never accepted as an argument, because arguments end up in shell history. Give the `NAME` and enter the value when asked, pipe it on stdin, or load a `.env` file with `--from-file`.

`miosa env info` masks variable values and never prints secret file contents. `--reveal` prints variable values and writes each reveal to the audit log.

## Repositories

```bash
miosa env repo add --env staging octocat/hello-world --branch develop --setup-file ./repo-setup.sh --blocking
```

`--source` selects `github` or `forge` (default `github`). `--blocking` means the machine is not usable until the setup script finishes; `--non-blocking` runs it alongside everything else.

## Toggles and protection

```bash
miosa env toggle --env staging github off
miosa env protect --env staging on
```

The four toggles are `github`, `secrets`, `machine-key` and `agent-connections`. `protect on` passes nothing of yours, whatever the toggles say. `miosa create --no-env` gives the same guarantee to one sandbox. `miosa env new --safe-for-third-parties` gives it to the environment itself.

## Versions and upgrades

```bash
miosa env versions staging     # how many machines sit on each version
miosa info my-box              # shows "staging v1", and whether an upgrade is available
miosa env upgrade my-box       # move one machine to the latest version
miosa env upgrade --all staging
```

Every save that changes what a machine receives creates a new immutable version. A machine pins the latest version when it starts and keeps it. Saving never reaches into a running machine.

> **Note**
>
> An upgrade is not reversible on the machine's disk. A secret the new version withholds is deleted from the machine, so `miosa env upgrade` asks you to confirm unless you pass `--force`.

## Start a machine from an environment

```bash
miosa create my-box --env staging
miosa computer create --env staging --size small
```

## Setup scripts

`--setup-file ./setup.sh` runs a script (UTF-8, at most 64KB) once, in the background, after the machine is ready. It never delays `ready`. Watch it with `miosa info`: the setup status is `pending`, `running`, `done` or `failed`, and a failed run shows its error. The CLI checks the size and encoding before it sends anything.

```bash
miosa create my-box --env staging --setup-file ./setup.sh
miosa info my-box
miosa env repo add --env staging octocat/hello-world --setup-file ./repo-setup.sh --blocking
```
cli/install:
`miosa` is the official MIOSA command line tool. There is one `miosa` CLI: version 2.3. It runs on macOS, Linux and Windows.

## 1. Install

**macOS / Linux**

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-cli-go/main/install.sh | sh
```

macOS and Linux. Installs to `~/.local/bin/miosa` for non-root users and `/usr/local/bin/miosa` for root. Override with `INSTALL_DIR=/usr/local/bin`.

**Windows**

```bash
npm i -g @miosa/cli
```

Installs the `miosa` 2.3 CLI. The package resolves the right native build for your platform, including Windows x64. Works the same on macOS, Linux and Windows.

The installer does these steps:

1. Detects your OS and CPU.
2. Downloads the matching `miosa` binary and checks its SHA-256.
3. Installs the binary onto your `$PATH`.

Then sign in with `miosa login` (step 3 below): it opens your browser, and the key for this machine is stored in `~/.miosa/config.toml`.

Prefer another install path?

**Homebrew**

```bash
brew install --cask Miosa-osa/homebrew-tap/miosa
```

macOS only.

**Manual**

Download the archive for your platform from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-cli-go/releases/latest) and place the binary in a directory on your `$PATH`.

```text
miosa_2.3.1_darwin_arm64.tar.gz
miosa_2.3.1_darwin_amd64.tar.gz
miosa_2.3.1_linux_arm64.tar.gz
miosa_2.3.1_linux_amd64.tar.gz
miosa_2.3.1_windows_amd64.zip
```

## 2. Verify

```bash
miosa --version
miosa version
```

These print `2.3.1`. If they print `1.x`, run `npm i -g @miosa/cli@latest` or `brew upgrade` to move onto the 2.x line.

## Windows

The npm install is the simplest path on Windows: `npm i -g @miosa/cli` resolves the `win32-x64` build (`@miosa/cli-win32-x64`) and puts `miosa` on your PATH.

To install by hand, download `miosa_2.3.1_windows_amd64.zip` from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-cli-go/releases/latest), extract `miosa.exe`, and add its folder to your `PATH`. In PowerShell:

```powershell
$dir = "$env:USERPROFILE\miosa"
Expand-Archive -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\miosa_2.3.1_windows_amd64.zip" -DestinationPath $dir
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "$env:Path;$dir", "User")

# open a new terminal, then
miosa --version
```

`SetEnvironmentVariable` with the `User` scope makes the change permanent without admin rights; it only affects terminals opened after you run it. For the current session only, use `$env:Path += ";$dir"` instead.

Windows builds are x64 only. There is no windows/arm64 archive.

## Upgrading from 1.x

1.x was the Node CLI. 2.x is the same `miosa` command with a rewritten command surface, and the installs above now all give you 2.3.x.

What changed:

- **Sandbox commands lost the `sandbox` prefix.** `miosa sandbox create` is now `miosa create`.
- **Deployment work moved under `miosa deploy`.** The old `miosa app` and top-level `releases`, `rollback` and `builds` commands are now `miosa deploy` subcommands. New in 2.2: `miosa deploy create` publishes a sandbox, a git repository or a local directory.
- **Contexts became profiles.** `miosa context` is now `miosa profile`, stored in `~/.miosa/config.toml`.
- **Restored in 2.1.** Several 1.x command families came back, renamed: `miosa device` (any runtime kind), `miosa mcp`, and the `miosa host` families for containers, meshes, GitHub Actions runners, backups and tunnels.
- **Still removed from the public CLI:** the internal OSA tooling `actions`, `blueprint`, `changes`, `drift`, `evidence`, `capabilities` and `command-overview`. Action authority is server-side, and `miosa --help` replaces `command-overview`.

## Update

```bash
miosa update            # download and replace the binary
miosa update --check    # report only
miosa version
```

`miosa update` verifies the SHA-256 of the download against the release `checksums.txt`, and refuses to replace a Homebrew-managed binary (use `brew upgrade` there). A one-line notice appears at most once a day when a newer version exists; silence it with `--no-update-notice` or `MIOSA_NO_UPDATE_NOTICE=1`.

## Shell completion

```bash
miosa completion zsh      # bash, fish, powershell
```

Sandbox names, profiles, templates and agents complete from the live API.

## 3. Sign in

```bash
miosa login               # opens the browser, device-code sign in
miosa whoami              # organization, plan, credits, and the scopes your key holds
```

`miosa whoami` shows the user, organization, workspace, plan and the scopes the key holds.

### Sign in with a key

`miosa login --with-key` asks for a key with hidden input, and `--key-stdin` reads it from stdin. A key is never accepted as an argument.

```bash
miosa login --with-key
echo "$MIOSA_KEY" | miosa login --key-stdin
```

### Credential resolution

Credentials resolve in this order:

1. `--api-key`
2. `MIOSA_API_KEY`
3. the active profile in `~/.miosa/config.toml`

> **Tip**
>
> CI and other non-interactive environments use `MIOSA_API_KEY`. See [Config and profiles](/docs/cli/config) for multi-account setups.

## Sign out

```bash
miosa logout
```

Removes the stored key of the active profile. `miosa logout --all` deletes the config file for every profile.

## Diagnose

```bash
miosa doctor
```

Checks configuration, connectivity and authentication, and prints a fix for each failure.

- [Config and profiles](/docs/cli/config): Named sign-ins, api_url, workspace defaults.
- [Raw API access](/docs/cli/api): miosa api for anything the high-level commands do not cover.
cli/machines:
A machine is either a sandbox (code and headless work) or a computer (a full GUI desktop). Lifecycle commands work on both.

## Create a sandbox

```bash
miosa create [name] [flags]
```

```bash
miosa create my-box --wait
miosa create ci-box --size small --template miosa-sandbox --ttl 2h --wait
miosa create my-box --env staging --setup-file ./setup.sh
```

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--size string` | `micro`, `tiny`, `xs`, `small`, `quad`, `medium`, `large`, `xl` (default `small`) |
| `--template string` | Template staged inside the sandbox image, for example `nextjs` or `static-html` (default `miosa-sandbox`) |
| `--env string` | Environment the sandbox starts from (default: your default environment) |
| `--no-env` | Pass nothing of yours to the sandbox (safe to hand to third parties) |
| `--setup-file string` | Shell script (UTF-8, max 64KB) run in the background once the sandbox is ready |
| `--ttl string` | Time to live: seconds, `90m`, `2h` or `2d` (default: the plan's) |
| `--idle-timeout string` | Pause after this much inactivity: seconds, `15m`, `1h` |
| `--meta stringArray` | Metadata, `KEY=VALUE` (repeatable) |
| `--workspace string` | Workspace slug to assign the sandbox to |
| `--wait` | Wait until the sandbox is ready for commands |
| `--wait-timeout duration` | How long `--wait` may take (default `3m0s`) |

## List and inspect

```bash
miosa list --state running
miosa list --json | jq -r '.data[].name'
miosa info my-box            # state, environment and setup status
miosa usage my-box           # runtime, time left and estimated cost
```

`miosa list` takes `--state`, `--tag`, `--template`, `--search`, `--workspace`, `--workspace-id`, `--limit`, `--page`, `--ids` (print only ids) and `--errored` (include sandboxes in the error state).

`miosa info` shows the pinned environment version (for example `staging v1`) and whether an upgrade is available.

## Current sandbox

```bash
miosa use my-box     # set the current sandbox
miosa use            # show it
miosa exec -- npm test
```

Anywhere a sandbox is expected you may give its name, its id, `current` or `self` (inside a sandbox).

## Start, stop, pause, resume, restart

```bash
miosa stop my-box     # keep the disk
miosa pause my-box    # keep disk and memory state
miosa resume my-box
miosa restart my-box --wait   # power-cycle in place: same id, same disk
```

`miosa restart` stops the sandbox keeping its disk and boots that disk again, so files, packages and enabled services survive and running processes start fresh.
Use it when a sandbox stops answering.
If its host stopped it with a memory checkpoint instead, the sandbox comes back from memory and the command says so, with the next step.

## Extend, tag and wait

```bash
miosa extend my-box --for 2h    # replace the time to live
miosa tag my-box --set team=ci
miosa wait my-box --for running
```

`miosa extend --for` accepts seconds, `90m`, `2h` or `2d`, and replaces the old value rather than adding to it.

## Fork and recover

```bash
miosa fork my-box copy-box      # a running copy of a sandbox
miosa recover my-box            # recover the disk into a NEW sandbox
```

## Destroy

```bash
miosa destroy my-box --yes
miosa destroy my-box other-box
```

`--yes` is required when there is no terminal. Destroy is permanent.

## Computers

Computers are the GUI machines. Every command that acts on one takes `--computer` where a machine argument appears.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `miosa computer create --size small` | Create a computer (`--size`, `--template`, `--env`, `--setup-file`) |
| `miosa computer list` | List computers |
| `miosa computer get <id>` | Details and status |
| `miosa computer start` / `stop` / `restart` | Power states |
| `miosa computer logs` | Recent VM-level logs |
| `miosa computer ports` / `urls` | Exposed ports and public URLs |
| `miosa computer auto-stop` | Auto-stop settings |
| `miosa computer rm --yes` | Destroy permanently |

> **Tip**
>
> To drive the desktop (screenshot, click, type), use an SDK or the MCP tools. The CLI exposes computer lifecycle, logs, ports and URLs. See [sdks overview](/docs/sdks).

## Deployments

```bash
miosa deploy create --from-sandbox <sandbox> --wait
miosa deploy create --git <url> --branch main --wait
miosa deploy create --dir ./dist --name my-site
miosa deploy                          # deploy the current directory
miosa deploy list
miosa deploy get <deployment>
miosa deploy logs <deployment> -n 200
miosa deploy env <deployment>          # environment variable names
miosa deploy env-set <deployment> --set KEY=VALUE
miosa deploy redeploy <deployment>
miosa deploy rollback <deployment> --to <version-id>
miosa deploy versions <deployment>
miosa deploy releases <deployment>
miosa deploy observe <deployment>
miosa deploy builds <deployment>       # build logs
miosa deploy requests <deployment>
miosa deploy promote <deployment>
miosa deploy stop <deployment> --yes
miosa deploy rm <deployment> --yes
miosa deploy domains <deployment>
miosa deploy domain-add <deployment> <domain>
miosa deploy domain-verify <deployment> <domain>
miosa deploy domain-rm <deployment> <domain>
```

`miosa deploy rollback --to` returns to a named version; without it, the previous one.

`miosa deploy env` lists the deployment's environment variable names. `miosa deploy env-set <deployment> --set KEY=VALUE` sets them, and values are encrypted at rest. `--set` is repeatable.

```bash
miosa deploy env my-app
miosa deploy env-set my-app --set DATABASE_URL=postgres://... --set LOG_LEVEL=info
```

### Create a deployment

`miosa deploy create` (alias `miosa deploy publish`) publishes a new deployment and makes it live. Give it one source:

- `--from-sandbox <sandbox>` publishes a running sandbox's output. Add `--port <n>` and `--run-command` to publish a running server, `--entrypoint <file>` to pick the entry file of a static publish, or `--type docker_deploy` for Docker Host.
- `--git <url>` connects a repository and queues its first build. Add `--branch` and `--build-command`.
- `--dir <path>` packages a local directory and uploads it, for pre-built static output with no repository.

With `--from-sandbox`, `--dir` is the path the app lives at inside the sandbox (default `/workspace`). On its own, `--dir` is a local directory to upload.

```bash
miosa deploy create --from-sandbox my-box --wait
miosa deploy create --from-sandbox my-box --port 3000 --run-command "npm start"
miosa deploy create --git https://github.com/me/app --branch main --wait
miosa deploy create --dir ./dist --name my-site
```

Common flags: `--name`, `--env KEY=VALUE` (repeatable, encrypted at rest), `--domain`, and `--wait` to block until the deployment is live and print its public URL. `--json` prints the result as JSON.

`miosa deploy` with no subcommand deploys the current directory: the git repository when the directory is one, otherwise a directory upload. It asks before publishing unless you pass `--yes`.

cli/scripting:
## Machine-readable output

`--json` (or `-o json`, or `MIOSA_OUTPUT=json`) prints machine-readable JSON on stdout.

```bash
miosa list --json | jq -r '.data[].name'
miosa create ci-box --wait --json | jq -r .id
```

Output is never switched to JSON automatically when piped. Commands that stream print one JSON object per line.

## Errors

Errors go to stderr with the API error code. With `--json` they are an `{"error":{...}}` object.

```bash
if ! miosa exec my-box --json -- ./flaky.sh > out.json 2> err.json; then
  jq -r '.error.code' err.json
fi
```

Destructive commands need `--yes` when there is no terminal.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Success |
| 1 | Error |
| 2 | Usage |
| 3 | Not signed in, or forbidden |
| 4 | Not found |
| 5 | Conflict or invalid input |
| 6 | Rate limited (after retries) |
| 7 | Server or network error |

`miosa exec` and `miosa ssh` exit with the remote command's status, so they drop straight into a pipeline:

```bash
miosa exec ci-box -- npm test || echo "tests failed with $?"
```

## Retries and timeouts

`--retries` (default 3) retries on 429 and transient 5xx. `--timeout` bounds a request in seconds, and for `exec` and `ssh` it also bounds the command (1 to 300).

## A CI pattern

```bash
export MIOSA_API_KEY="$MIOSA_CI_KEY"
miosa create "ci-${CI_PIPELINE_ID}" --size small --ttl 1h --wait --json | jq -r .id
miosa exec "ci-${CI_PIPELINE_ID}" -- ./build.sh
status=$?
miosa destroy "ci-${CI_PIPELINE_ID}" --yes
exit $status
```

## Raw calls from scripts

`miosa api` uses the same credentials and prints the body:

```bash
miosa api GET /sandboxes/ci-box/ports --json | jq -r '.data[].port'
miosa api POST /webhooks -d @hook.json
```

> **Tip**
>
> For non-interactive use, set `MIOSA_API_KEY` and avoid browser login entirely. See [Config and profiles](/docs/cli/config) for profiles and credential order.
cli/snapshots:
## Snapshots

`miosa snapshot` works on sandboxes and computers alike. Every snapshot of a machine is its history. A named snapshot is a restore point you pin on purpose: it outlives the machine and never appears in history. Each organization keeps 10 named snapshots free.

```bash
miosa snapshot list my-box
miosa snapshot save my-box before-upgrade
miosa snapshot fork before-upgrade
miosa snapshot latest my-box
```

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `miosa snapshot list [machine]` | History across machines, or for one; `--search`, `--workspace`, `--limit` |
| `miosa snapshot named` | Named snapshots and the free allowance |
| `miosa snapshot save <machine> <name>` | Pin a machine (running: captured now, stopped: its newest snapshot) under a name |
| `miosa snapshot save --snapshot <id> <name>` | Pin one existing snapshot |
| `miosa snapshot rm <name>` | Remove a name |
| `miosa snapshot latest <machine>` | Newest snapshot of a machine |
| `miosa snapshot info <id>` | One snapshot and what depends on it |
| `miosa snapshot tree <id> [path]` | List files inside a snapshot, machine stopped or gone |
| `miosa snapshot pull <id> <path> -d ./out` | Download a file, or a folder (extracted from a tar), without overwriting |
| `miosa snapshot fork <id>` | New machine from a snapshot |
| `miosa snapshot fork --name <name>` | New machine from a named snapshot |
| `miosa snapshot delete <id>... \| --all <machine>` | Delete what you name; anything still depended on is skipped and reported |

Deleting needs `--yes` when there is no terminal. Use `--computer` when the machine argument is a computer. `miosa snapshot save` captures a running machine now (waiting with `--wait`, on by default) or the newest snapshot of a stopped one.

## Checkpoints

Checkpoints are sandbox-local restore points.

```bash
miosa checkpoint create my-box --comment "before deps"
miosa checkpoint list my-box
miosa checkpoint info <checkpoint>
miosa checkpoint delete <checkpoint>
```

## Restore

```bash
miosa restore my-box <checkpoint>
```

Restores a sandbox from a checkpoint.

> **Tip**
>
> Snapshots are the portable, cross-machine history and the basis for forking. Checkpoints are the quick sandbox-local restore points. Use `miosa snapshot` when you want to move or fork a machine, and `miosa checkpoint` for a fast rollback in place.

## exec

```bash
miosa exec [name|id] -- <cmd> [args...] [flags]
```

Run a command inside a sandbox and print its output. `miosa` exits with the remote command's exit code, so it drops straight into scripts and CI. The `--` separator is required before the command.

```bash
miosa exec my-box -- echo hello
miosa exec -- ls -la /home                              # uses the current sandbox
miosa exec my-box --cwd my-repo -- npm run build
miosa exec my-box -- bash -c 'for i in 1 2 3; do echo $i; done'
```

`--cwd` sets the working directory, relative to the sandbox home directory (or absolute).
`exec` streams output until the command finishes.
For work that runs a long time, start it in the background so it keeps running after you disconnect.

A sandbox that is still starting refuses commands. `exec` retries with backoff until it is ready, up to 90 seconds.

## ssh

```bash
miosa ssh my-box
miosa ssh my-box -- bash -lc "cd app && npm test"
miosa ssh my-box -- bash -s < ./setup.sh
```

`miosa ssh` runs the system `ssh` through the authenticated tunnel with a one-time key and a short-lived certificate (15 minutes, valid for that sandbox only). Where the server has no certificate authority it authorizes the one-time key in the sandbox instead. The key, certificate and host file live in a private temporary directory removed when ssh ends.

Standard input is piped through, up to 80KB. `--api` runs the command over the MIOSA API instead, and so does a machine without `ssh`. There is no interactive login shell yet.

`ssh user@host` and `scp` against a sandbox directly do not work: there is no public SSH endpoint.

## console

```bash
miosa console my-box
```

An interactive shell in a sandbox using the miosa-terminal-v1 WebSocket relay, with a real PTY, resize handling and the remote exit code.

## files

```bash
miosa files [command]
```

Remote paths are written `<sandbox>:<path>`. The sandbox may be a name or id, and can be omitted for the current sandbox. Relative remote paths start in `/home/user`.

```bash
miosa files ls my-box:/workspace
miosa files cp ./app.py my-box:/workspace/app.py
miosa files cp -r ./src my-box:/workspace/
miosa files cp my-box:/workspace/out.json ./out.json
miosa files cat my-box:/workspace/out.json
cat config.yaml | miosa files write my-box:/workspace/config.yaml
```

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `files ls [-l] <path>` | List a directory (`-l` shows modification times) |
| `files cp [-r] <src> <dst>` | Copy local to remote, remote to local, or remote to remote |
| `files cat <path>` | Print a file |
| `files write <path>` | Write stdin to a file, creating parent directories |
| `files mkdir <path>` | Create a directory and its parents |
| `files mv <from> <to>` | Move or rename (alias `rename`) |
| `files rm [-r] [-f] <path>...` | Delete files or directories |
| `files chmod <mode> <path>` | Change permissions (octal, for example `755`) |
| `files stat <path>` | Type, size, mode and modification time |

A directory needs `-r`. A path that does not exist is an error unless `-f` is given.

## Background processes

```bash
miosa process start --name build --cwd /workspace/app -- npm run build
miosa process list
miosa ps
miosa process logs <pid> --tail 50
miosa process kill <pid>
miosa process get <pid>
```

`miosa ps` is the same as `miosa process list`.

## Daemons

A sandbox daemon is a named long-lived process: start it with a name, then read
its output, restart it or stop it by that name.

```bash
miosa daemon create my-box --name web --command "npm run dev" --cwd /workspace/app
miosa daemon list my-box
miosa daemon logs my-box web
miosa daemon restart my-box web
miosa daemon stop my-box web
```

Named services belong to a Computer, where systemd owns them; `miosa services`
is the project Services command and does not take sandbox flags.

## Logs and events

```bash
miosa logs my-box -n 100 -f     # system log, follow
miosa events my-box             # stream lifecycle events
```

## Ports, previews and URLs

```bash
miosa ports my-box
miosa preview create my-box 3000 --visibility public
miosa preview list
miosa url my-box
```

`miosa preview` publishes a sandbox port at a public URL and is where visibility
is decided: `--visibility private|public`, `--ttl`, `--name`. `miosa url` prints
the URL a sandbox's endpoint answers on, and `miosa preview unshare` revokes a
public link.

## Proxy

```bash
miosa proxy my-box 5432:5432
```

Forwards local ports to sandbox ports over a WebSocket tunnel (any TCP service; the key needs `sandboxes:exec`).

## Desktop

```bash
miosa desktop start my-box
miosa desktop url my-box
```

> **Note**
>
> Running a command over the API and over ssh have the same exit-code behaviour: both exit with the remote command's status.
